newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - D.Telekom tops up issue on big demand.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - D.Telekom tops up issue on big demand.

text.p: Europe's largest-ever public offering of shares got even bigger as Deutsche Telekom responded to overwhelming investor demand on Monday by topping up its stock offer with 100 million additional shares.

The initial public offering (IPO), to begin next week when shares start trading in Germany, New York and Tokyo, swells to as much as 18 billion marks ($12 billion) from 15 billion previously or as many as 690 million shares.
Speculation is running high that the offering could be oversubscribed as much as six times because of a storm of orders from private investors.

Many of these investors are first-time buyers of stocks who have caught the "stock market fever" causing normally cautious German savers to cast aside aversions to risk and take a chance on cashing in on Telekom's privatisation.

"The initial placement of Deutsche Telekom will become a milestone for German stock markets. I am convinced that the offering will be a huge success," said Telekom management board chairman Ron Sommer.

Priced at between 25 and 30 marks per share, Telekom's IPO will put around 23 percent of its total equity capital in the hands of public investors. The German government will initially retain the remaining 77 percent of the company's shares.
Telekom said it would now float 600 million shares with a face value of five marks a share to the public, when trading begins on November 18.
The company also fattened its Greenshoe option, or overallotment, to 90 million shares, up from 75 million shares previously.
The Greenshoe allows the managing banks -- Deutsche Bank, Dresdner Bank and Goldman Sachs -- to float additional shares to satisfy demand and keep the share price from rising too high too quickly.
The share offer will be carried out through a capital increase. Deutsche Telekom will raise its capital by three billion marks, up from 2.5 billion previously.

As Telekom's only shareholder, the German government has declined to subscribe to the new shares, allowing Telekom to offer them to the public. The subscription period, which began on October 22, ends on November 14.
The government has given Telekom the green light to raise its capital by five billion marks to the year 2000.
The flotation now of additional shares will mean that a second flotation, expected in around two years, will be that much smaller, a Telekom spokesman said.
Independent of the global offering, Telekom also increased the number of shares it is offering to its employees to 30 million from 20 million previously.

Telekom said it topped up the offering because of "strong global demand" for its shares. But the groundswell of interest on the part of private German investors was probably the most significant catalyst for the additional offering.

More than three million Germans signed up with the company's share information centre to take advantage of the discounted share price and special loyalty bonuses for investors who hold their "T-shares" at least three years.

Because of the huge public response, it has been widely believed that institutional investors would not be able to order as many shares as they would like, forcing them to buy more shares on the open market.

This in turn could create a shortage of Telekom shares and drive up the share price in the early phase of trading. Telekom said the additional shares would be alloted proportionally among German and foreign investors and institutional and private investors.
